_podcast.theme_scoring_prompt:
Rate how well this article fits the theme 'Indigenous Lands & Innovation' — Indigenous nations using technology, governance, and stewardship on their own terms.

OUT OF SCOPE — score 0-9: geopolitical and war news with no Indigenous rights angle; general wildfire and wildlife-service updates not led by or directly affecting Indigenous communities or guardians; provincial forestry and environmental policy with no explicit First Nations involvement; consumer tech and gadget reviews; science with no Indigenous stewardship or sovereignty context; crime and judicial news unrelated to Indigenous rights.

CALIBRATION — apply this ladder to everything else. Indigenous-led journalism on governance, rights, and self-determination is a strong fit on its own: a technology hook raises a score but is NOT required to reach the top band.
- 80-100: Excellent Indigenous-led reporting. Cariboo stories bridging governance or culture AND technology land here (Tŝilhqot'in/Secwépemc/Dakelh language revitalization tech, guardian programs using sensors and drones, GIS land mapping, Indigenous-led connectivity, digital heritage projects) — and so does outstanding national coverage of sovereignty, treaty, and land rights.
- 55-79: Solid pan-Canadian Indigenous governance, sovereignty, land rights, treaty, or reconciliation journalism — APTN, Eagle Feather News, or IndigiNews-style coverage of First Nations governance, MMIWG, land claims, self-determination, and Indigenous-led services. Most Indigenous governance journalism belongs HERE, not below.
- 30-54: Indigenous cultural, community, or human-interest stories (awards, events, ceremonies) with limited governance substance, or BC land-stewardship and environmental stories with meaningful First Nations involvement.
- 10-29: General BC land, environmental, or forestry stories that mention Indigenous communities only in passing.

ANCHORS: 'Tŝilhqot'in Nation launches drone-based caribou monitoring on title lands' → 98. 'First Nations leaders reject BC's revised land-title framework' → 75. 'Secwépemc language app reaches 1,000 learners' → 88. 'BC Wildfire Service updates evacuation alerts for the Interior' → 8.

Score 0-100 where 100 is a perfect thematic match and 0 is completely unrelated.

items.title: [Fast Company] Investors push back on SEC plan to release corporate earnings less frequently
items.content_html:
🪶 ✏️

The U.S. government has pitched an obscure accounting rule change that has ignited a firestorm of opposition. If enacted, its effects might be felt from the capital markets to your retirement savings account.

At issue is a proposal by the Securities and Exchange Commission that would scrap a long-standing requirement for registered companies to disclose their earnings every three months. Instead, they would have the option to do so only every six months.

The agency says its proposal has two goals: One is to reduce a company’s compliance costs needed to prepare financial statements; the other is to promote longer-term planning rather than a short-term fixation on earnings. A final decision is expected by late 2026.

These ideas may sound in the weeds to the average American, but the proposal has prompted opposition that is literally record-breaking ever since it was released for comments in May 2026. To date, more than 280,000 letters have come in, with the vast majority against. By comparison, one study that covered 417 different proposals over 30 years tallied more than 65,000 letters total.

I’m an accounting professor who has constructed a tracker that lets people scour the SEC docket and decipher the general sentiment of these comments. I found that the main driver of this hostility is concern that less-frequent reporting would make it harder for investors to monitor companies’ performance and decision-making, because key information is withheld for longer periods.

This reduction in transparency carries another risk as well: It would likely make it more expensive for companies to raise capital. Once external monitoring is reduced, investors may demand a higher rate of return because they have less information about a company’s health. That means companies would need to pay more for that uncertainty, whether through selling shares, borrowing from lenders, or issuing bonds.

In short, there’s a trade-off between the cost of capital and transparency.

A tsunami of opposition

If a business wants to be a publicly traded company, it has to register with the SEC, which governs and regulates this process. Once registered, the company has to disclose its financial performance every three months, a requirement that has held since 1970.

Whenever the agency issues a new rule, it opens it up to comments first, just like other government agencies do. That feedback is meant to shape the final rule before it becomes codified.

What’s unusual in this case is the overwhelming degree of opposition—more than 99% of all comments, many from retail and individual investors, according to my tracker.

“My husband worked for Enron. We lost most of our retirement savings when their fraudulent activity came to light,” wrote one commenter. “We were still young enough to make some of that income back, but we knew many retirees who ended up working into their 80’s. Quarterly reporting is a gate keeper. Keep it.”

Wrote another: “I rely on quarterly reporting for the same reason your child gets a quarterly report card. . . . There the metaphor ends, because a good teacher can catch failing performance and course correct with parents long before report cards are issued. Investors do not have that luxury.”

Some point out that the commission’s claim of company savings on compliance costs is overblown. The estimated average savings, according to the proposal, is around $200,000 a year per firm, which is a drop in the bucket for a typical public corporation.

But more broadly, the comments reveal how much this rule could matter to ordinary investors. Retirement savings, through 401(k) plans and individual retirement accounts, are directly exposed to company performance, whether or not the fund in question is diversified. That means any reduction in financial transparency has direct implications on how the investments of the funds are monitored.

That risk was laid out in a letter from the Securities Industry and Financial Markets Association, or SIFMA. The trade group wrote that the estimated net savings “could be offset or outweighed by an increase in the cost of capital as investors demand higher risk premia for less timely information.”

Federated Hermes, an asset manager, also pointed to this scenario: “Issuers that elect semiannual reporting may face signaling risks, as investors could interpret such a choice as reflecting reduced transparency. This may affect analyst coverage and cost of capital.”

Companies weigh in

As for the companies themselves, it’s too early to say whether they would take advantage of the six-month option. But several have said they would choose to report less frequently.

Drugmaker Eli Lilly is one example, making clear its preference in its official comment, while letters from Financial Executives International, an industry lobby, stated that 58% of the member companies it surveyed suggested they would change.

For its part, the commission is still evaluating all the feedback before its leadership takes a vote. Traditionally, it’s led by five commissioners, with three representing the party in power and two from the opposition. In this case, however, the two Democratic seats in the minority are currently vacant, and one Republican seat is about to be vacated.

With so few votes on hand, the commission may in fact change its rules so that this proposal could clear with support from only two commissioners. On September 30, 2026, it suggested a rule change so that the two votes would suffice.

For now, SEC Chair Paul Atkins seems undeterred and has stated that the commission is moving ahead.

How many companies will make the move given the concerns laid out in the comments, however, remains an open question.

As the SEC’s own Investor Advisory Committee, an independent body, put it: “The evidence does not support the view that short-termism is a major problem for U.S. public companies today, nor is there strong evidence to support the view that costs for public companies would be significantly reduced.”

Tzachi Zach is a professor of accounting at The Ohio State University.

Scientists in Vienna have achieved a major breakthrough in timekeeping by creating the world’s first self-stabilizing nuclear clock, a technology that could eventually surpass even the most precise atomic clocks. Instead of relying on electrons in atoms, the clock uses the tiny nuclei of thorium atoms, which are far less sensitive to outside disturbances.

items.title: [Fast Company] A new employee was reprimanded for drinking 1 cup of coffee a day. An expert says the drink isn’t the real problem
items.content_html:
🪶 ✏️

A new employee says they were reprimanded for drinking too much coffee.

The user took to Reddit to detail the situation, which unfolded at a job they’d started only a month prior. Each morning, they used the coffee machine and company-provided K-Cups and creamers. However, one day, a floor manager called them in and told them it was not typical to drink coffee every single morning. 

“I don’t imagine my boss having anything to say that would make this situation better, and I think it would just be unnecessary trouble,” the user wrote. “I do not want to be seen as someone who picks problems with people for small things.” 

To mitigate the problem, the new employee said they will bring their own K-Cups and creamers into the office moving forward. They also plan to document future interactions with the manager. “I need this job more than anything right now so I’m willing to look the other way since I’m not in the position at the moment to make any demands,” they said. 

Office culture

Many of the user’s fellow Redditors immediately sided with them.

“Even when free, I’ve never once heard of a single person being told they’re drinking too much. Especially not at one per day; that seems bizarre,” wrote one user.

Another commented, “As an intern, I was drinking five cups a day, and nobody batted an eye. It got to the point where the office manager told me where to restock the coffee pods if I saw we were running low. This is a super weird thing for them to be concerned about.” 

Experts say the user’s now-lingering tension over coffee usage could potentially lead to a deeper issue around comfort and safety at the workplace.

According to data from a national study by the Harris Poll, 60% of American workers report currently having a toxic supervisor, with more than 60% admitting they actively avoid their boss at work. 

“This type of behavior dramatically reduces psychological safety at that workplace. As a result, that new employee is more likely to quit and more likely to engage in activity to damage the company’s reputation,” Russell Clayton, an associate professor of instruction in the School of Management at the University of South Florida, told Inc. 

According to the Harris Poll, 61% of workers plan to switch jobs because of their boss as soon as the market allows. A separate survey done by the MIT Sloan Management Review analyzed 34 million employee profiles and found that toxic culture was the strongest predictor of employee attrition and was 10.4 times more important than compensation in predicting turnover.  

Get 1 Smart Business Story delivered straight to your inbox when you subscribe to Inc.’s free daily newsletter.

—By Moses Jeanfrancois, News Writer

This article originally appeared on Fast Company’s sister website, Inc.com.

items.title: [Fast Company] What to think about before making a big ask from your direct reports
items.content_html:
🪶 ✏️

As a supervisor, you have some ability to dictate what your direct reports work on. The requests you make should typically fit their job description, though most descriptions have a catchall “other duties as assigned” attached, which is likely to cover you.

That said, the jobs you give someone generally have a particular expectation of the skills required, the hours to be worked, and the stress level associated with the tasks. If you’re going to ask someone to do something that far exceeds the norm, there are a few things you should consider first.

Are you taking advantage?

The people you supervise probably want to keep you happy. You have power over their evaluations, and your recommendation can help to propel them to a promotion or other opportunities. This means that when you ask your reports to do something, they are likely to agree.

You should make sure that when you’re making a big ask, the employee is likely to benefit rather than suffer from doing the work. For example, you have work that needs to be done, but you don’t want to put the time of a higher-priced employee onto it. If you’re going to try to save money by using a less-experienced person, you should be careful that you’re not adding a lot of extra hours or stress to their work just to cut costs.

Your reports pay attention to the hours that other people are putting in. If you ask far greater effort of them than you put in yourself, that can rankle in ways that may ultimately cause dedicated people to want to work elsewhere.

What are the long-term benefits?

When you are going to make that big ask, think about what benefits that work is likely to have for your direct report. Talk to them about those benefits when you make the request.

For example, a big project may give a newer employee a chance to work with senior leaders, or do work that is visible to them. That can help bring them future opportunities. A significant project may also help them to expand their capacities by taking on new experiences. That project may also lead to overtime (depending on how they are paid), allowing them to take home more money.

One reason for thinking through the benefits of this additional work for an employee is that you may discover that the assignment might be more beneficial for another member of your team. The more you can use significant tasks to develop your team, the easier it is to ask them to go beyond the norm.

What will sweeten the deal?

Of course, there are also some pretty onerous tasks that someone has to take on—and you may decide that burden should fall on one of your team members. In this situation, consider whether there are ways to make the burden less significant.

If the job is going to require additional travel or a lot of extra hours, you might want to offer compensatory time off or some time with a flexible work arrangement to reward them for taking one for the team.

If you’re going to give a team member a significant responsibility that adds effort and stress to their work, consider ways to help use that to further their career. Give that person additional mentorship to accelerate their career path or provide them with chances to engage with senior leaders who might ultimately be able to find additional opportunities for them.

When you use big asks as a way to give flexibility or career benefit to your team members, you create trust. The members of your team will talk to each other, and you don’t want to get the reputation of someone who drives people hard without looking out for them. When you give people challenge as well as support, you provide a motivating environment that allows the team to excel, even under difficult circumstances.

The study, published Sept. 30 in the Journal of Happiness Studies, surveyed adults ages 18 to 34 [scitechdaily.com#1]. The findings show associations, not proof that childhood experiences caused adult outcomes: participants recalled their upbringing and reported their current well-being [scitechdaily.com#1]. Separately, a review of fatherhood research described links between sustained positive father involvement and children’s cognitive, social and emotional outcomes, while noting that the findings were correlational [time.com#1].
